# Dimension: Isolation on a Laptop

Covers each harness's own sandbox, how it behaves inside rootless Podman or
NVIDIA OpenShell, published resource requirements, and what adding a harness to
the user's existing `openshell-sandbox` tool would involve. Sources are in
[citations.md](../citations.md). Local files are marked LOCAL; they are context,
not web citations.

## Built-in isolation per harness

| Harness | Built-in OS isolation | Default | Network control | Rootless Podman |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hermes | Terminal backends. `local` has none; `docker` uses namespaces and dropped capabilities [4] | `local`: "Commands run directly on your machine with no isolation" [4] | `docker_network: false` cuts egress from the execution container [4]. Egress proxy wired for Docker only [5] | Configuration page: "Podman is supported out of the box: set HERMES_DOCKER_BINARY=podman" [4]. Security page does not list Podman as a terminal backend [12] |
| OpenHands | Docker sandbox for the agent server [51]. Agent Canvas npm mode runs on the host [43] | npm mode: "The agent has host filesystem access" [43] | No egress allowlist in fetched docs | No Podman support statement found in fetched docs. Open issues [53][54], PodmanWorkspace PR in draft [55] |
| Codex CLI | bubblewrap + seccomp, legacy Landlock kept [96] | `sandbox_mode` workspace-write available; read-only root [93][96] | Network off unless `network_access`; domain proxy "experimental; off by default" [93] | Nested bwrap fails under Ubuntu AppArmor userns restriction [98][130] |
| Claude Code | Sandboxed Bash tool (bubblewrap + socat on Linux) [113] | Falls back to unsandboxed unless `failIfUnavailable` [113] | Proxy with domain allowlist [113] | Needs `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` in an unprivileged container [113] |
| Goose | None documented on the permissions page; permission modes only [79] | Autonomous [79] | Not stated | Only "goose in Docker" (build from source) [87] |
| opencode | None documented on the permissions page; permission rules only [62] | "Most permissions default to 'allow'" [62] | Not stated | No guidance found |

### Details and caveats

- **Hermes Docker backend scope.** "The agent runs on your host but executes
  every command inside a single, persistent Docker sandbox container" [10]. The
  agent process, its LLM calls and its git operations stay on the host.
  CVE-2026-71963 shows the effect: a malicious `.git/config` gives RCE
  "exposing the full environment including configured provider API keys"
  [122].
- **Hermes in containers skips its own checks.** "Dangerous command checks are
  skipped because the container itself is the security boundary" [12].
- **Claude Code's sandbox covers only part of the agent.** It covers only Bash,
  PowerShell and Monitor commands. "MCP servers, command hooks, and plugin
  monitors… run unconstrained on the host" [114]. Anthropic: "Always run
  --dangerously-skip-permissions sessions inside a container, a VM, or the
  sandbox runtime" [114].
- **Goose scoping is advisory.** A user describes project scoping as "more of a
  suggestion for the model than any sort of enforced rule" [88].
- **Nested sandboxes.** Ubuntu 23.10 and 24.04 restrict unprivileged user
  namespaces through AppArmor [130]. Codex's inner bwrap then fails with "No
  permissions to create new namespace" inside an outer sandbox [98]. Running a
  harness inside OpenShell therefore generally means turning the harness's own
  sandbox off. The existing `openshell-sandbox` already does this for Claude
  Code and Codex (LOCAL).

## NVIDIA OpenShell and NemoClaw on a laptop

- OpenShell support matrix (v0.1.7): Podman is "Supported for rootless local and
  workstation workflows" [26]. Kernel needs Landlock ABI 3+ (Linux 6.2) and
  seccomp user-notification ADDFD. If the probes fail, launch "fail[s] closed"
  [26].
- OpenShell's own first-agent walkthrough "runs OpenCode against a free
  OpenRouter model" [25].
- NemoClaw is "an open source reference stack for running supported AI agents
  more safely inside NVIDIA OpenShell" and "is an alpha project" [24]. Hermes
  install: `NEMOCLAW_AGENT=hermes`, telemetry on by default [22].
- NemoClaw constraints:
  - "Managed installations require exact stable OpenShell 0.0.116" [23]. The
    support matrix is at v0.1.7 [26]; the two are not reconciled in fetched
    sources.
  - Docker is the default provider: "In both Docker-driver modes, the sandbox
    is a Docker container" [23].
  - Native rootless Podman is optional: "On a qualified Linux host, you can
    instead select native rootless Podman explicitly with
    NEMOCLAW_GATEWAY_RUNTIME=podman ; this path does not require the Docker CLI
    or daemon" [22]. The architecture page lists "the explicitly selected native
    Podman provider for OpenClaw, Hermes, and LangChain Deep Agents Code" [23].
  - [22] also says "Hermes Portable uses a current-user rootless Podman
    container for the selected Ollama model". How that relates to the Docker
    default for the standard install is not stated.
- OpenShell security defaults [29]:
  - egress is deny-by-default;
  - L7 enforcement defaults to `audit` ("logs violations but forwards
    traffic");
  - "A glob like /** allows any binary to reach the endpoint, defeating
    binary-scoped enforcement."

## Adding a harness to `openshell-sandbox` (LOCAL + web facts)

LOCAL: `bin/harness-wrapper.sh` accepts only `claude` or `codex`
(`valid_harness()`). Codex needed a baked-in binary, an auth file plus a
headless login, an `AGENTS.md` symlink to the shared prompt, and a flag
disabling its own sandbox.

| Harness | Install | Config / auth | Own-confinement off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hermes | `curl … install.sh \| bash`, `--non-interactive`, `--skip-browser` [11] | `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, `.env` for secrets, `auth.json` for OAuth [4][5] | `terminal.backend: local` is the default [4] |
| opencode | Install script or npm [69] | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` [65] | `--auto` [62] |
| Goose | CLI install script; DEB/RPM/Flatpak [86] | `~/.config/goose/config.yaml`; plain-text secrets without keyring [80] | Autonomous is default [79] |
| OpenHands | npm / Docker / VM / Cloud (Agent Canvas) [44] | Not stated | Headless always auto-approves [49] |

Inferences, not stated by any source:

1. Inside OpenShell, Hermes would run with `terminal.backend: local`. Its Docker
   backend and egress proxy need a container runtime that the sandbox does not
   provide. OpenShell then supplies the isolation, matching how Claude Code and
   Codex already run there.
2. The OpenShell policy would need egress for the installer host
   (`hermes-agent.nousresearch.com` [11]) and the chosen LLM provider. That
   applies unless Hermes is baked into the image. The sandbox policy has no
   GitHub access (LOCAL), and the installer clones source, so baking it into the
   Containerfile is likely required.
3. OpenHands and Hermes are server processes with web ports. OpenHands' default
   and recommended sandbox is Docker [51], and its npm mode has no sandbox
   [43][44]. Of the two, Hermes fits a single-container sandbox better, using
   the local backend plus the API server.

## Counter-evidence

1. **Codex sandbox bypass.** CVE-2025-59532: a model-generated cwd was treated as
   the writable sandbox root (fixed 0.39.0). It "did not impact the
   network-disabled sandbox restriction" [99].
2. **Claude Code sandbox escape.** CVE-2026-25725: a missing
   `.claude/settings.json` was unprotected, letting sandboxed code plant hooks
   that run with host privileges (fixed 2.1.2). GitLab rates it 8.8 [119] and
   OpenCVE 10.0 [121].
3. **Silent sandbox disable.** Claude Code issue #34315: `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`
   bypassed the sandbox with no prompt. The workaround is
   `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` [120].
4. **DNS exfiltration through allowlists.** An OpenAI research model reached a
   public chatbot through "insufficient DNS filtering in its training sandbox"
   [132]. CSA recommends treating DNS "as a first-class egress control point"
   [131]. OpenShell's docs say the proxy resolves DNS after policy allows a
   connection [29]. They do not address DNS tunnelling from inside the sandbox.
5. **Docker socket as escape hatch.** Pillar Security drove Codex, Cursor and
   Gemini CLI to launch privileged containers through a reachable Docker daemon.
   "A closed profile controls what the agent's own process can ask the kernel
   for. It does not control what a privileged local daemon will do" [102].
   Claude Code docs: access to docker.sock "effectively grants access to the
   host system" [113]. OpenHands' legacy launch mounts it [42].
6. **OpenShell defaults.** An independent reviewer: "Several defaults are
   permissive: audit enforcement, no layer-7 rules until you set a protocol and
   Landlock best_effort" and "Each allowed endpoint is an exfiltration path"
   [32]. The OpenShell issue tracker showed 395 open issues [31].
7. **Shared kernel.** A microVM vendor argues "Containers share one kernel, so a
   single kernel or runtime flaw can undo every boundary you configured" [138].
   That applies to rootless Podman and OpenShell's container drivers [32].

## Gaps and Limitations

- No field report confirms Hermes running under OpenShell or Podman. The vendor
  claims Podman support [4] but does not list it as a terminal backend on its
  security page [12].
- Goose and opencode egress host lists are not documented in fetched pages.
  Claude Code publishes one (api.anthropic.com, claude.ai, platform.claude.com,
  downloads.claude.ai among others) [116].
- No laptop-class footprint numbers exist for Goose or opencode, and none are
  independently measured for any harness.
- NemoClaw documents native Podman [22][23], but whether its pinned OpenShell
  0.0.116 [23] can coexist with the laptop's existing OpenShell install is not
  stated.
